title: Poker
intro: Poker is a family of card games in which players bet on who holds the best hand, and in which a player can win without the best hand by betting so that everyone else gives up. That mix of chance, hidden information and betting makes it a game of decisions under uncertainty: the cards decide single hands, but over thousands of hands the money flows to the players who make better decisions. This topic starts with the rules and builds up to the mathematics strong players use: probability, pot odds and expected value, ranges, game theory, tournament equity and the statistics of winning and losing.

items: Rules, hands and betting: how a hand of Texas hold'em is dealt and bet, how hands rank, the betting structures, positions and the other popular forms of poker. Start here if you are new. See #/poker/rules.

Cards, combinations and probability: counting starting hands and combinations, outs and the rule of 4 and 2, the chance of flopping a set or a flush draw, and how one hand fares against another. See #/poker/probability.
Pot odds, equity and expected value: when a call pays, implied odds, fold equity, and the thresholds every bet size sets for both players. See #/poker/pot-odds-and-ev.

Strategy before and after the flop: opening ranges by position, three-bets, continuation bets, board texture, bet sizing, value bets and bluffs, and how to read opponents and their statistics. See #/poker/strategy.

Ranges, game theory and solvers: thinking in ranges, range and nut advantage, polarised and capped ranges, the Nash equilibrium of poker (GTO play), toy games that show where the bluffing frequencies come from, and how solvers find strategies. See #/poker/game-theory.
Tournaments and ICM: why tournament chips are not money, the Independent Chip Model, bubble factors, push-or-fold play with short stacks, and bounties. See #/poker/tournaments.
Variance, win rates and bankroll: how far luck can carry results, how many hands it takes to know a win rate, the risk of ruin, and bankroll management. See #/poker/variance-and-bankroll.

blocks.text: Why poker is a game of skill and of luck

In any one hand the cards can beat the best decision: a player who gets all their chips in with an 80% favourite still loses one time in five. That is the luck. The skill is in choosing actions whose average result is best, which poker players call making positive expected value (+EV) decisions. A good decision that loses is still a good decision, and a bad decision that wins is still a bad one. Judging a play by its result rather than by its expected value is called results-oriented thinking, and avoiding it is the first habit of a strong player.

David Sklansky put the aim another way in his Fundamental Theorem of Poker: every time you play a hand differently from the way you would have played it if you could see your opponents' cards, they gain; every time you play it the same way, you gain. You cannot see their cards, so you work with the next best thing: the set of hands they could hold, weighted by how likely each is. That set is a range, and almost all advanced poker thinking is about ranges.
The three ideas that run through everything

items: Expected value. The average result of a decision over all the ways it could turn out. Every choice (fold, call, raise, and how much) has one, and the best choice is the one with the highest. See #/poker/pot-odds-and-ev.

Ranges. You never put an opponent on one hand; you put them on a range and update it as they act. Your own range matters as much: what you would do with every hand you could hold here decides how hard you are to play against. See #/poker/game-theory.

Position. The player who acts last on each betting round sees what everyone else does before deciding. That information is worth so much that strong players play many more hands from late position than from early. See #/poker/rules and #/poker/strategy.

blocks.text: Notation used on these pages: ranks are A K Q J T 9 ... 2 (T is ten), suits are s h d c (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs). A specific hand is written like AhKd; a kind of hand like AK, AKs (suited, both cards the same suit) or AKo (offsuit). Amounts are usually given in big blinds (bb), the size of the big forced bet, so that the same ideas apply at every stake.

Poker is a standard example of a game of imperfect information, the kind studied in game theory (see #/game-theory). Unlike chess, a player does not know the full state of the game, so the best strategy has to be mixed: it must sometimes bluff and sometimes call with weak hands, in proportions that leave the opponent nothing to exploit. Researchers have used poker as a test problem for decades. A program called Cepheus essentially solved heads-up limit hold'em in 2015, and the programs Libratus (2017, heads-up no-limit) and Pluribus (2019, six players) beat top professionals. Their methods now underpin the solver software players study with, described on #/poker/game-theory.
